meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Hale. Was Owen heard before you entered that zero?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
"Pretty conclusive." That's a machine's guess, and the people who sell these tools say in print not to punish a student on that alone. You didn't answer me: did anyone speak to Owen first?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. So what do you have besides the software?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.

I'm writing those times down. He told me he wrote it over the weekend, and a student who drafts somewhere else and pastes it in looks exactly like that. Did you ask him where he drafted it before you entered the mark?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
I've read the scene, and it isn't there. A seventeen-year-old who gets a quotation wrong loses marks for it; he doesn't get a zero. And you still haven't told me whether you spoke to him first.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their minds between an outline and an essay; that's what an outline is for. Hale, I asked whether you spoke to Owen and you keep handing me paper. I'm taking that as a no.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

So you did speak to him. Five minutes after class, in your own notes, and a seventeen-year-old on the spot said "like, being stuck," which is not far off. I'll want those notes and the September 24 piece in an email tonight.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That is what 4.4 says. He'll do the rewrite, to put this behind him and for no other reason, and the new mark is in the gradebook well before December 1. Tonight, in writing, with the line that nothing goes on his file.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school, and nobody in his class hears a word about why. I'll be reading your email tonight.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes. A private, supervised rewrite on Thursday, its mark replaces the zero, nothing goes on his record, and I have all of it in writing tonight. Ten minutes, if there's anything else.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

cc: the principal

Hale,

You agreed today that Owen will do a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, that its mark will replace the zero and be entered well before December 1, and that nothing goes on his record. I still require that agreement in writing, including the line that nothing goes on his file, together with your notes from November 2 and his in-class writing from September 24. I expect all of it tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: Last position. She agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants that in writing tonight along with your November 2 notes and the September 24 writing; that is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and you reached it before her time ran out.
What moved her: You told her you had spoken to Owen on November 2 and showed notes written that day, which answered the procedural question she kept returning to with a dated document she could read herself.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it close to conclusive, which handed her a machine's opinion she had come prepared to dismiss and left her first question unanswered.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked. Your version history, with the essay arriving in two large edits between 11:52 PM and 11:58 PM on Wednesday, October 28, came very close to a night like that, though nothing said in the meeting tied it to the same one. It proves nothing about the essay; it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked in her first line whether Owen had been heard before the zero, answer with the November 2 conversation and your dated notes straight away instead of leading with the checker score.
